# Introduction - Motivation
Every year college football teams a few hundred thousand dollars to millions on recruiting. This number has only gotten higher as NIL laws of changed as well as being able to legally pay athletes. But does this extra expense really pay off? Does the increase in recruiting power really lead to more on field success? To look at this question we pull data from a [college football data API](collegefootballdata.com). To answer this question we will use recruiting rank and win percentage. 

## Ethical Consideration
Before webscraping it is always important to read the terms of service to understand what data can and cannot be accessed and if the data is able to be published to a GitHub repository. In this case, getting the API is free and immediate, however, the company does still want web scraping to come from this and to be able to control who has access to the data and who does not. For this specific API, they request that the data is not published on public repositories. Thus, here we will walk through the steps for you obtain your own API key and then pull your own data. Please be respectful when using this API and follow the terms and service.

# College Football API Access and Use
To begin, go to [CollegeFootballData API](collegefootballdata.com) where you can submit your email to get your personalized API key. The email should come through immediately. Once you have your API key you can begin!

To follow along with more in-depth code use this [GitHub repository](https://github.com/hnpeterson8/data_acquisition_blog_code). Begin with cloning the repo and then we can start pulling the data from the API

To ensure that we do not publish our API key to GitHub, put the following code in your `.env` and ensure that `.env` is in your `.gitignore`: `API_KEY = {your_api_key}`. Next, using the `requests` library, queried the `/recruiting/teams` and `/records` endpoints for seasons 2018 through 2024, looping through each year with a polite 0.5-second delay. The resulting JSON responses were flattened into pandas DataFrames using `pd.json_normalize()` and merged on team name and season. 

```python
import os
import pandas as pd
import requests

# Load API key securely from environment variables
api_key = os.getenv("CFBD_API_KEY")
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}

# Request recruiting data for a target season
url = "[https://api.collegefootballdata.com/recruiting/teams](https://api.collegefootballdata.com/recruiting/teams)"
params = {"year": 2023}

response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, params=params)

if response.status_code == 200:
    # Flatten nested JSON into a clean tabular DataFrame
    recruiting_df = pd.json_normalize(response.json())
    print(recruiting_df[["team", "points", "rank"]].head())
```
In the full pipeline script (available in the project repository - file `acquire_data.qmd`), this request is wrapped inside a loop over seasons 2018 through 2024, paired with a polite `time.sleep(0.5)` delay between requests. A matching loop pulls win-loss records from the `/records` endpoint. This dataset does not have a variable that has the win percentage but it can be easily calculated as `wins/games` or the number of wins divided by the number of games played. Some basic data cleaning is necessary to ensure that variable naming convention is the same across the two datasets so that merging can happen properly. To finish creating the final dataset, we use `pd.concat()` to join the datasets on `['team', 'year']`. 


# EDA: Win-Percentage vs. Recruiting Rank
Once we have the data, we can load it into a new script where we can do exploratory data analysis. To follow along with more in-depth EDA, use the `eda.qmd` file in the referenced GitHub repository. Here we will just go through the highlights of the analysis.

## Scatterplot
```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# load in the data
data = pd.read_csv("data/college_football.csv")

# plot of win pct vs recruiting rank
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(data["win_pct"], data["recruiting_rank"], c = data["year"], alpha = 0.65)
ax.set(xlabel="Win Percentage",
       ylabel="Recruiting Rank", title="Win-Percentage vs. Recruiting Rank")
plt.show()
``` 

This graph shows the win percentage vs recruiting rank and is colored by year. It is hard to see any real differences by year. In the EDA file, I break up this graph by year to be able see differences in trends. The graph does show a slight negative correlation between the two variables. Lets explore this next. 

## Correlation By Year
```{python}
# correlation between win percentage and recruiting rank
# in theory we should see a negative correlation (higher rank corresponds to lower number)
## see if there is difference by year
year_corr = (
    data.groupby("year")
    .apply(
        lambda g: g["win_pct"].corr(g["recruiting_rank"]),
        include_groups=False,
    )
    .reset_index(name="corr")
)
# print output
print(year_corr)
```

Based on the year by year correlations, each year sees a weak negative correlation. 2020 sees the weakest correlation but that could be due to this being the Covid year and so the seasons were shorter and structured differently than other years.

## Correlation By Conference
Correlation by year tells us generally which years had better success from recruiting, but it does not tell us the full story. What if we want to know are certain conferences better at turning recruitment into success? Below we look at the correlation between win percentage and recruiting rank based on conferences. 
```{python}
## look how it works within conferences
conf_corr = (
    data.groupby("conference")
    .apply(
        lambda g: g["win_pct"].corr(g["recruiting_rank"]),
        include_groups=False,
    )
    .reset_index(name="corr")
)

# print output
print(conf_corr)
```

As can be seen, conferences like the SEC, NEC (Northeast conference), FCS Independents (not technically a conference, but grouped together as one), and Big 10 have much stronger correlations of -0.5 or lower (closer to -1). These conferences are getting better results likely related to their recruiting rank, indicating that they are better at turning recruitment into success. While some conferences like AWC, Atlantic Sun, and OVC actually have medium strength positive correlation. For these conferences, they are not affectively using recruiting for success. 

## Top 10 and Bottom 10 
Finally, one might want to know how well the top and bottom 10 in recruiting ranking do in terms of win percentage. Since the ranking is done each year, we will look at the teams that are in the top 10 and bottom 10 for each of the years, respectively. For the top 10, there are 17 unique teams across the 7 years. This generally makes sense that those that would be in the top 10 are often consistently in the top 10 based on budgets. Another consideration is that this in the middle of the new NIL rules which allowed for athletes to be paid. This changed how recruiting works pretty substantially where teams were allowed to pay recruits, within school budgets, which meant that it was no longer just the top teams doing it under the table. It to some degree leveled the playing field. That is, however, the top conferences stayed the top conferences. There were only 6 unique conferences within the top 10, again pushing the idea that the top stays the top. 

On the flip side we see the bottom 10. Here there are 57 unique teams and 18 unique conferences. Some of this could be due to conference realignment and whatnot but there is also the element that schools that just can't pay their athletes the same amount will have lower rankings. Thus we see more variation in the bottom 10.
